title: Occam's Razor
body: The principle is attributed to the 14th-century philosopher William of Ockham: do not assume more entities than necessary. It is still used as a rule of thumb for choosing the simplest explanation that fits the facts.

title: The Categorical Imperative
body: In 1785 Immanuel Kant set out a moral rule that holds regardless of one's goals: act only on a principle you could will to become a universal law. It is the cornerstone of duty-based, or deontological, ethics.

title: The Four Noble Truths
body: The core of Buddhism: life involves suffering, suffering arises from craving, suffering can end, and the way to end it is the Noble Eightfold Path. The teaching is attributed to the Buddha's first sermon.

title: I Think, Therefore I Am
body: René Descartes sought knowledge that could not be doubted and concluded that the act of doubting proves one's own existence. The argument appears in his Discourse on the Method of 1637 and became a foundation of rationalist philosophy.

title: Socrates
body: Socrates wrote nothing himself; we know him mainly through Plato's dialogues. He questioned people to expose contradictions in their beliefs. In 399 BC he was sentenced to death in Athens for corrupting the young and impiety.

title: The Five Pillars of Islam
body: The five basic duties of Islam are the declaration of faith, the daily prayers, almsgiving (zakat), fasting during Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to Mecca for those able to make it.

title: Confucianism
body: Confucius lived in China in the 6th and 5th centuries BC. His teaching stresses moral cultivation, respect within family and social relationships, and the ruler's duty to lead by example. It shaped Chinese government and culture for over two thousand years.

title: Plato's Allegory of the Cave
body: In the Republic, Plato describes prisoners who see only shadows on a cave wall and take them for reality. The allegory illustrates his view that the senses show us mere appearances, while true knowledge concerns unchanging Forms.

title: Utilitarianism
body: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill argued that the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number. Utilitarianism is the best-known form of consequentialism, which judges actions by their outcomes.

title: The Social Contract
body: Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651), John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau (The Social Contract, 1762) explained political authority as an agreement among individuals. They disagreed on what people give up and what they keep, but the idea underpins modern theories of legitimate government.

title: Stoicism
body: Founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens around 300 BC, Stoicism teaches that virtue is the only true good and that we should focus on what is within our control. Epictetus, Seneca and the emperor Marcus Aurelius are its best-known Roman voices.

title: Existentialism
body: Jean-Paul Sartre summed up existentialism as 'existence precedes essence': humans are not born with a fixed nature but define themselves through their choices. Søren Kierkegaard in the 19th century is often seen as its forerunner.

title: Karma and Samsara
body: In Hinduism, the soul passes through a cycle of rebirth, samsara, shaped by karma, the moral consequences of actions. The ultimate goal is moksha, liberation from the cycle. Key texts include the Vedas, the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita.

title: The Great Schism of 1054
body: In 1054 mutual excommunications marked the split between the Church of Rome and the Church of Constantinople. The division into the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, rooted in disputes over authority and doctrine, persists today.

title: Aristotle's Golden Mean
body: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle argued that virtue lies between two extremes: courage, for example, between cowardice and recklessness. His virtue ethics focuses on character rather than rules or consequences.

title: Brahman and Atman in the Upanishads
body: The Upanishads, philosophical texts of ancient India whose earliest parts date from the first millennium BC, explore the nature of reality and the self. Their central insight is that atman, the innermost self, is identical with Brahman, the ultimate reality underlying the universe, an idea expressed in the phrase 'tat tvam asi', 'that thou art'. Realising this identity is seen as the path to liberation.

title: Calvinism
body: John Calvin (1509–1564), a French theologian who led the Reformation in Geneva, set out his theology in the Institutes of the Christian Religion. He stressed God's absolute sovereignty and predestination, the belief that God has chosen in advance who will be saved. Calvinism spread to the Netherlands, Scotland, France and New England, shaping the Reformed and Presbyterian churches; Max Weber later linked its ethic to the rise of capitalism.

title: Laozi and the Daodejing
body: The Daodejing, traditionally attributed to the sage Laozi, is the founding text of Daoism. It teaches that the Dao, the 'Way' underlying all things, cannot be fully put into words, and that wisdom lies in simplicity and wu wei, effortless action in harmony with nature. Whether Laozi was a historical person is uncertain, and the text probably took shape over several centuries BC.

title: Nietzsche and the Death of God
body: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) declared that 'God is dead': belief in God had lost its hold on modern Europe, undermining the values built upon it. He attacked Christian morality as a 'slave morality' born of resentment and called for a revaluation of all values, embodied in the figure of the Übermensch. After his death his sister promoted a distorted, nationalist reading of his work.

title: Maimonides
body: Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), born in Córdoba, became the leading Jewish thinker of the Middle Ages and a court physician in Cairo. His Mishneh Torah systematically codified Jewish law, and his Guide for the Perplexed sought to reconcile Jewish faith with Aristotelian philosophy. His thirteen principles of faith became a standard summary of Jewish belief, and he influenced Christian scholars including Thomas Aquinas.

title: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex
body: In The Second Sex (1949), Simone de Beauvoir argued that woman has been defined as the 'Other' in relation to man, and that 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman'. Applying existentialist ideas to women's situation, she showed how femininity is shaped by society rather than nature. The book became a founding text of modern feminism.

title: Inca Religion
body: Inca religion honoured Inti, the sun god, from whom the Sapa Inca, the emperor, claimed descent, alongside the creator god Viracocha and Pachamama, the earth mother. The Coricancha temple in Cusco, adorned with gold, was its centre. Sacred places and objects called huacas, from mountains to the mummies of ancestors, were venerated across the empire, and Andean beliefs survived the Spanish conquest blended with Catholicism.

title: Mencius and Human Goodness
body: Mencius, a Confucian thinker of the 4th century BC, argued that human nature is fundamentally good. Everyone, he said, has 'sprouts' of virtue, such as the instinctive alarm at seeing a child about to fall into a well, which must be cultivated. His later rival Xunzi held the opposite view, but Chinese tradition came to rank Mencius second only to Confucius.

title: Mana and Tapu in Polynesia
body: Mana and tapu are key concepts across Polynesian cultures. Mana is spiritual power, authority and prestige, which can be inherited, gained or lost; tapu marks people, places and things as sacred or set apart, and breaking it brought danger. The English word 'taboo' entered the language after Captain James Cook recorded it in Tonga in 1777.

title: Abraham and the Abrahamic Religions
body: Abraham is revered as a founding patriarch by Judaism, Christianity and Islam, which are therefore called the Abrahamic religions. In Genesis, God calls him to leave Mesopotamia for Canaan and makes a covenant promising him countless descendants. In Islam he is Ibrahim, a prophet who with his son Ismail built the Kaaba in Mecca. Historians cannot confirm that he existed.

title: Erasmus and Christian Humanism
body: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (died 1536) was the leading figure of northern Renaissance humanism, which sought to renew learning and Christian life by returning to classical and biblical sources. He published an edition of the Greek New Testament in 1516 and mocked the abuses of the clergy in The Praise of Folly. Though he criticised the Church, he refused to join Luther's break with Rome.

title: Ma'at in Ancient Egypt
body: In ancient Egyptian religion, Ma'at was both a goddess and the principle of truth, justice and cosmic order. The pharaoh's central duty was to uphold ma'at against chaos. In the judgement of the dead, as depicted in the Book of the Dead, a person's heart was weighed against the feather of Ma'at, and only a heart in balance could pass into the afterlife.

title: Aquinas's Five Ways
body: Thomas Aquinas (around 1225–1274), a Dominican friar, combined Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology in his unfinished Summa Theologiae. In it he offered five ways of showing that God exists, arguing from motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection and the order of nature. He held that reason and faith cannot truly conflict, and his synthesis became central to Catholic teaching.

title: Nagarjuna and Emptiness
body: Nagarjuna, an Indian monk who probably lived in the 2nd century AD, founded the Madhyamaka, or 'Middle Way', school of Mahayana Buddhism. He argued that all things are empty (shunyata) of independent, inherent existence, because everything arises in dependence on other things. He is often considered the most important Buddhist philosopher after the Buddha himself.

title: The Aztec Fifth Sun
body: The Aztecs believed the world had been created and destroyed four times and that they lived in the age of the Fifth Sun, which would also end in catastrophe. The gods had sacrificed themselves to set the sun in motion, so humans owed them a debt to be repaid in blood. This belief underpinned the human sacrifices at the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan, dedicated to the war god Huitzilopochtli and the rain god Tlaloc.

title: Heraclitus and Flux
body: Heraclitus of Ephesus, active around 500 BC, taught that everything is in flux, an idea summed up in the saying attributed to him that you cannot step into the same river twice. He held that the world is a unity of opposites in constant tension, ordered by the logos, a rational principle. His near-contemporary Parmenides argued that change is an illusion, and their clash shaped Greek metaphysics.

title: The Four Aims of Hindu Life
body: Classical Hindu thought names four legitimate goals of human life, the purusharthas: dharma (duty and righteousness), artha (wealth and power), kama (pleasure and love) and moksha (liberation from rebirth). The first three are to be pursued in balance, with dharma guiding the others, while moksha is the highest goal. The scheme frames classical Indian works from the Arthashastra on statecraft to the Kamasutra.

title: The Trolley Problem
body: In 1967 the British philosopher Philippa Foot posed a dilemma: a runaway tram will kill five people unless it is diverted onto a track where it will kill one. Most people think diverting it is permissible, yet few approve of pushing someone into its path to save five, though the numbers are the same. Developed further by Judith Jarvis Thomson, the 'trolley problem' probes the moral difference between killing and letting die, or intending and foreseeing harm.

title: Shinto
body: Shinto is the indigenous religion of Japan, centred on the worship of kami, spirits present in nature, places, ancestors and outstanding people. It has no founder or single scripture and focuses on ritual purity, shrines and festivals. For centuries it coexisted and blended with Buddhism, and from the Meiji period until 1945 a state form of Shinto was promoted to support the cult of the emperor.

title: Popper and Falsifiability
body: Karl Popper (1902–1994) argued that what distinguishes science from non-science is not that its theories can be proved but that they can be falsified: a scientific theory makes predictions that could turn out wrong. No number of white swans proves that all swans are white, but one black swan disproves it. On this basis he criticised Marxism and psychoanalysis as unfalsifiable.

title: The Prophet Muhammad and the Hijra
body: Muhammad (around 570–632), born in Mecca, is regarded by Muslims as the final prophet of God. From around 610 he reported revelations that were later collected as the Quran. Facing hostility in Mecca, he and his followers migrated to Medina in 622, the Hijra, which marks year one of the Islamic calendar. By his death he had united much of Arabia under Islam.

title: Augustine of Hippo
body: Augustine (354–430), born in Roman North Africa, became bishop of Hippo, in present-day Algeria, and the most influential theologian of the Latin West. His Confessions, an account of his restless path to Christianity, is often called the first Western autobiography. In The City of God, written after the sack of Rome in 410, he contrasted the earthly city with the heavenly one, and his teaching on original sin and grace shaped both Catholic and Protestant thought.

title: The Golden Rule
body: The Golden Rule, treating others as one would wish to be treated, appears in many traditions. Confucius stated it in negative form ('Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself'), as did the Jewish sage Hillel, while Jesus put it positively in the Sermon on the Mount. Its recurrence across cultures makes it a common reference point in ethics, though philosophers note that people's wishes differ.

title: Kuhn's Paradigm Shifts
body: In The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), Thomas Kuhn argued that science does not progress by steady accumulation. Periods of 'normal science' work within a paradigm, a shared framework of theories and methods, until anomalies pile up and a revolution replaces it, as when Copernican astronomy displaced the Ptolemaic system. The term 'paradigm shift' passed into everyday language.

title: Paul the Apostle
body: Paul of Tarsus, a Jewish Pharisee who had persecuted Jesus's followers, became Christianity's most influential missionary after a vision of the risen Christ. In the AD 40s and 50s he travelled through Asia Minor and Greece, founding communities that welcomed non-Jews without requiring them to follow Jewish law. His letters are the earliest surviving Christian writings and form a large part of the New Testament.

title: Guru Nanak and Sikhism
body: Sikhism was founded in the Punjab by Guru Nanak (1469–1539), who taught devotion to one formless God, the equality of all people regardless of caste, and honest work and service to others. He was followed by nine human gurus; the tenth, Gobind Singh, declared that the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the eternal Guru. The Golden Temple at Amritsar is the faith's holiest shrine.

title: Pyrrho and Ancient Scepticism
body: Pyrrho of Elis, who travelled with Alexander the Great as far as India, is regarded as the founder of Greek scepticism. Pyrrhonists argued that for every claim an equally strong counter-argument can be found, so one should suspend judgement, which they believed brings tranquillity. Preserved in the writings of Sextus Empiricus, these arguments were rediscovered in the Renaissance and influenced Montaigne and Descartes.

title: Zen Buddhism
body: Zen, known in China as Chan, is a school of Mahayana Buddhism that stresses meditation and direct insight over the study of scriptures. It took shape in China in the 6th to 8th centuries and spread to Korea, Vietnam and Japan, where it flourished from the late 12th century. Its teachers used paradoxical riddles called koans to break habitual thinking, and it deeply influenced East Asian painting, poetry and gardens.

title: Historical Materialism
body: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels argued that history is driven by material and economic conditions rather than by ideas. Each society's forces and relations of production, its economic 'base', shape its laws, politics and beliefs, the 'superstructure'. Conflict between classes, they held, moves history through stages from slavery and feudalism to capitalism and, they predicted, communism.

title: The I Ching
body: The I Ching, or Book of Changes, is one of the oldest Chinese classics. Its core is a system of 64 hexagrams, figures of six broken or unbroken lines, used for divination, to which philosophical commentaries were later added. It became one of the Confucian classics, and it later fascinated Western thinkers such as Leibniz and Carl Jung.

title: The Rule of St Benedict
body: In the 6th century Benedict of Nursia wrote a rule for his monastery at Monte Cassino, in Italy, organising monks' days around communal prayer, manual work and reading under the authority of an abbot. Moderate rather than extreme in its demands, it became the basis of monastic life in the Latin West. Benedictine monasteries preserved learning and copied classical texts through the early Middle Ages.

title: Mahayana Buddhism and the Bodhisattva
body: Mahayana, the 'Great Vehicle', emerged in India around the beginning of the common era and became the main form of Buddhism in China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Tibet. Its ideal is the bodhisattva, who seeks enlightenment out of compassion and vows to help all beings reach liberation, not only themselves. Mahayana also introduced new scriptures, such as the Lotus Sutra and the Heart Sutra.

title: Islam in Southeast Asia
body: Islam spread to Southeast Asia mainly through trade rather than conquest, carried by Muslim merchants from Arabia, India and elsewhere along Indian Ocean routes. From the late 13th century rulers in northern Sumatra, and later the port city of Malacca, adopted Islam, and it spread across the Malay world and Java. Southeast Asian Islam was often shaped by Sufism and blended with local traditions.

title: The Bhagavad Gita
body: The Bhagavad Gita, 'Song of the Lord', is a 700-verse dialogue within the Indian epic the Mahabharata. On the eve of battle the warrior Arjuna hesitates to fight his kinsmen, and his charioteer Krishna, revealed as a form of the god Vishnu, teaches him to do his duty without attachment to its results. It presents paths to liberation through action, knowledge and devotion, and is one of Hinduism's most widely read scriptures.

title: Pascal's Wager
body: Blaise Pascal, the 17th-century French mathematician, argued in his Pensées that belief in God is a rational bet. If God exists, the believer gains infinite happiness; if not, little is lost, whereas the unbeliever risks infinite loss. Critics object that one cannot simply choose to believe and that the wager ignores the many possible gods, but it was an early use of the reasoning of decision theory.

title: The Hebrew Bible
body: The Hebrew Bible, or Tanakh, is the scripture of Judaism and, as the Old Testament, part of the Christian Bible. Its name comes from its three parts: Torah (the five books of Moses), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings). Composed and edited over many centuries, largely in the first millennium BC, it tells of creation, God's covenant with Israel, the Exodus and the history of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

title: The Aboriginal Dreaming
body: For Aboriginal Australians, the Dreaming (an English term; each language has its own word) is the creative era when ancestral beings shaped the land, created life and laid down law, and also their continuing presence. Dreaming stories, songs and ceremonies bind people to particular places and govern kinship, conduct and responsibilities for land. The ancestral tracks across the country, often called songlines, also serve as maps.

title: Democritus and Atomism
body: In the 5th century BC Leucippus and his pupil Democritus proposed that everything consists of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms, from the Greek for 'uncuttable', moving in empty space. Differences between things arise from the shapes, sizes and arrangements of their atoms. Taken up by Epicurus and the Roman poet Lucretius, the theory was speculative rather than experimental, but it anticipated modern atomic theory.
